newsitem.title: USA: Bottom-fishers prop dlr off lows at US midday.
newsitem.headline: Bottom-fishers prop dlr off lows at US midday.

text.p: The dollar struggled up from session lows at midday, catching a solid bid from bottom-fishers after a heavy bout of profit-taking sent the greenback nearly two pfennigs below a fresh 94-month peak against the mark in morning trade.
The greenback had pushed as high as 1.8913 marks in European dealings, but ran out of steam as U.S. trading got underway -- continuing a trend which has persisted throughout the week.
"It seems as though the market was a little over-exuberant at the upper end of the trading range," said John Nelson, foreign exchange trading manager at ABN-AMRO Bank in Chicago.

At midday, the dollar was changing hands at 1.8790/00 marks, down from 1.8860/70 at the open, but up from its low of 1.8739 reach in the late morning. Sterling was trading at $1.6008/15 after slumping over three cents to a low of $1.5918 and opening at $1.5958/63.
And against the yen, the dollar was near its lows of the day, hit by comments from U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky.
Barshefsky repeated that the U.S. was concerned with a sharp drop in automotive sales to Japan and warned Japan not to export its way out of its current economic malaise.

The remarks followed comments from Lawrence Greenwood, economic minister-counsellor at the U.S. embassy in Tokyo, who said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television that rises in Japan's current account surplus had the potential to create an explosive situation with the United States.
"I think some clouds are gathering on the horizon on the trade front and that could cause problems for the dollar up here," said Brian McCarthy, analyst at Ruesch International.
Dealers said the market was cautious ahead of the Friday release of Japanese current account data for June.
At noon, the dollar was trading at 118.65/75 yen versus 119.46/51 at the open.

Dealers attributed sterling's sharp overseas fall to repositioning by large hedge funds ahead of the Bank of England's Thursday decision on interest rates, and said the move was exacerbated by a technical breakdown which set off stop-loss sell orders below $1.6150 and $1.60.
Many economists were still banking on higher UK rates on Thursday, though some conceded that recent pound strength could give the central bank reason to think twice about such a move.
"We've accumulated some evidence in recent months that sterling is having a sufficiently serious effect on the British economy to warrant holding off on raising rates," said McCarthy.

A substantial rise in German joblessness for July and the Bundesbank's addition of a net 2.6 billion marks at its weekly repo auction were taken as signals by the market that German officials were neither ready nor well-positioned to defend their ailing currency through higher interest rates.
Remarks from a German government spokesman, who said Bonn saw no reason to change its stance on foreign exchange developments, also reassured dollar/mark bulls overseas.
Traders warned against reading too much into the dollar's morning weakness on Wednesday and said the U.S. currency was still on track to test 1.90 marks this week.
"At any moment we can take a three-to-four pfennig correction in the dollar and it won't mean anything," said Robert Sabia, vice president at ING Barings Capital Markets.

Elsewhere on Wednesday, the dollar drifted down to 1.5305/15 Swiss francs at midday after opening at 1.5345/55. It also slumped over two centimes to 6.3435/65 French francs from 6.3670/00 at the open after popping to another near-eight year peak of 6.3802 in Europe.
At midday, the greenback had climbed to Canadian $1.3855/60 from C$1.3826/31.
(( -- Noah Barkin, N.A. Forex Unit, 212-859-1673 ))
